title: You can be right… and still be wrong.
paragraphs: You can be right… and still be wrong.
You can preach boldly… and still be missing something.
And that’s where it gets dangerous.
Because the scariest place to be is not rebellion.
It’s partial truth with full confidence.
Scripture says he was eloquent, mighty in the Scriptures, and fervent in spirit (Acts 18:24–25).
That means he knew the Word.
And here’s the open loop most people miss:
What if the thing holding you back is not your sin…
…but your pride hiding inside your gifting?
What if you’re not stuck because you don’t know enough…
…but because you think you already do?
Because this is where the tension rises.
We live in a generation that celebrates visibility over humility.
If you sound confident, people assume you’re correct.
If you speak loudly, people assume you’re an authority.
If you have a platform, people assume you’re anointed.
But heaven does not measure like that.
God is not impressed with volume.
And Apollos gives us a mirror we don’t always want to look into.
Because many of us are like him.
We drop Bible verses in comment sections.
We speak in the name of God.
There are areas in our life where we are still inaccurate.
Some of us don’t reject correction because it’s wrong.
We reject it because it threatens our image.
Because deep down, we’ve built an identity around being “the one who knows.”
And when someone like Priscilla and Aquila comes—quiet, faithful, not flashy—and says, “Let me show you more…”
And pride will keep you spiritually stuck while making you look spiritually active.
Now here is the Scripture that cuts through all of it:
“He began to speak boldly in the synagogue, but when Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately.” — Acts 18:26
That’s the miracle in the story.
Not just that he was taught.
Some scholars interpret this moment as a turning point in Apollos’ ministry—because after this, he becomes even more effective, powerfully refuting error and strengthening believers (Acts 18:27–28).
This is not just about Apollos.
About that quiet place in your heart where you don’t want to be corrected.
That area in your life where you say, “I already know that.”
That relationship where someone tried to speak truth, and you shut down.
God cannot fully use the version of you that refuses to be taught.
Not because He doesn’t love you.
And without formation, there is no transformation.
Because this is not just about behavior.
The Bible says, “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.” (James 4:6)
That means pride doesn’t just slow your growth.
It puts you in resistance against God Himself.
And here is where Jesus enters the story.
Because none of us are just “slightly inaccurate.”
The root issue is not lack of knowledge.
It is a heart that wants control.
A heart that says, “I’ll follow God… but on my terms.”
And sin separates us from God (Romans 3:23).
No amount of gifting can fix that.
But to save us from ourselves.
Jesus, the perfect Son of God, lived without sin, yet humbled Himself to the point of death on a cross (Philippians 2:8).
He took our pride, our rebellion, our hidden resistance—and paid for it with His blood.
So that we could be forgiven.
At the cross, you don’t have to pretend you know everything.
You don’t have to defend your image.
You don’t have to hide your gaps.
And Jesus does not reject you.
He begins to teach you more accurately.
Will you let God correct you?
Will you let Him send people into your life to sharpen you?
Will you surrender the need to always be right?
Will you lay down your pride at the feet of Jesus?
Because on the other side of humility…
Where are you hiding behind knowledge?
Where has pride quietly taken root?
“Lord, teach me. Even when it hurts. Even when it humbles me. I surrender.”
Because the safest place you can be…
If this pierced your heart, don’t ignore it.
